rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s matching name and opening with its predecessor signal a shared subject; the coming passage will disclose it and summarize the preceding Hāmīm sūrahs.
rows.anchor: the fact that this sūrah also begins with the same name and the same opening verses shows that both sūrahs have something in common

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse expresses sorrow over people who stubbornly deny the scripture and evade the warning God revealed through it.
rows.anchor: This is an expression of sorrow on people who are adamant on denying the noble scripture revealed by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning they evade is the Day of Judgement; denying it would make the universe seem purposeless, contrary to its Creator’s wisdom.
rows.anchor: refer to the Day of Judgement. Such is the nature of this reality that if it is not accepted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe displays both divine power and wisdom; when attributes appear without a conjunction, they coexist in the one they qualify.
rows.anchor: when attributes are mentioned without a particle of conjunction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A purposeful universe must have an appointed end, followed by a court of justice that rewards good deeds and punishes evil ones.
rows.anchor: an obvious consequence of its purposefulness is that it should exist till a certain time period and not go on forever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because deeds propagate effects across generations, final justice requires gathering their farthest consequences and all relevant testimony, including records from nature, at a universal Judgment.
rows.anchor: every deed of a person whether it is a pious one or an evil one has the ability in it to be contagious

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good and evil actions leave far-reaching effects; a final Judgment must disclose those effects and present every witness needed for complete justice.
rows.anchor: if it is needed that a person be given true information of his good and evil deeds, then it is essential

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since complete testimony requires all humanity and potentially the records of heaven and earth, the world must end and all people face one court.
rows.anchor: This, of course, can only be possible when the Day of Judgement is common to all

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idolaters evade the warning because they rely on alleged deities and intercessors, imagining these beings can save them at Judgment.
rows.anchor: since they rely on their alleged deities and intercessors, they do not pay heed to the warnings of the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge asks whether the objects of worship created any part of earth or share in creating the heavens; without such a role they cannot be partners in God’s sovereignty.
rows.anchor: they can only deserve to be called partners of God if they have any role in the creation of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument relies on common ground: Arabian idolaters themselves acknowledged God as Creator of everything.
rows.anchor: the idolaters of Arabia regarded God to be the Creator of everything. Thus this argument is based on something which they too acknowledged

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic term athārah denotes an inherited tradition transmitted from forefathers, as defined in Aqrab al-mawārid.
rows.anchor: refers to a tradition which is transmitted from someone’s forefathers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A claim that God has partners can be settled only by God’s own testimony, known through revelation or faithfully transmitted tradition; conjecture cannot justify it.
rows.anchor: whether God has a partner or not is an issue which can only be resolved through God’s testimony

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Torah, Gospel, and other scriptures suffered interpolations, neither they nor transmitted accounts of Abraham and earlier prophets contain evidence of polytheism.
rows.anchor: Though the Torah, the Gospel and other scriptures have been inflicted with large-scale interpolations yet they contain no trace of polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabian idolaters claimed ancestral precedent, but repeated Qur’anic challenges could not elicit any religious or rational basis for their practice.
rows.anchor: they were unable to prove if their ways had a religious or rational basis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s qualifying words require inherited tradition to rest on knowledge rather than fancy or conjecture.
rows.anchor: The words which qualify it are meant to show that this tradition should be based on knowledge and not on fancy or conjecture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who invoke beings other than God are deeply astray: the invoked cannot answer and are unaware, then become their worshippers’ enemies at Judgment.
rows.anchor: more unfortunate or farther in error than those who invoke and beseech others than God who will never be able to respond

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imaginary deities cannot know that they are invoked; real beings such as angels, jinn, or Jesus likewise cannot hear or accept such worship.
rows.anchor: The beings which the Idolaters worshipped were either fictitious so that the question of being informed of invocations of the worshippers does not even arise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s account in al-Mā’idah has Jesus deny teaching people to worship him and his mother, saying he knew nothing of their conduct after his death.
rows.anchor: God will ask Jesus (sws) on the Day of Judgement if he had taught people to worship him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Furqān depicts the angels denying that they misled worshippers and explaining that people forgot God’s reminder after receiving His favors.
rows.anchor: They will answer: “Glory be to You! It was not befitting for us to choose other guardians besides You

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets and righteous people will hold accountable those who made them divine partners in defiance of their teachings.
rows.anchor: as far as the prophets and the righteous are concerned, they will hold those people responsible who made them partners of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinn and devils will disown their worshippers, who will curse them; Islahi directs readers to his discussion of al-Qaṣaṣ 62–64 for details.
rows.anchor: they will be the greatest enemies of their worshippers, let alone bringing benefit to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse introduces the excuses idolaters invent to evade the Qur’an’s call.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the various excuses which these Idolaters would invent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When unable to answer clear Qur’anic arguments on monotheism and the Hereafter, the deniers call the Qur’an magic; Quraysh leaders acknowledged its force but dismissed it as verbal sorcery.
rows.anchor: when the very clear verses of the Qur’ ān relating to monotheism and the Hereafter are recited before them, and they do not have any answer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the truth magic after it has arrived condemns deliberate deceivers: before clarity someone may be mistaken, but thereafter only those seeking to mislead themselves and others make excuses.
rows.anchor: once it becomes evident, only those people make such excuses who want to live in deception and want to lead others to deception as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusation that the Prophet fabricated revelation is baseless, so the discourse conveys astonishment and leaves the case to God rather than debating it.
rows.anchor: Since this was an absolutely baseless propaganda and its baseless nature was fully evident to its perpetrators

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Prophet invented the Qur’an and falsely attributed it to God, God’s punishment would overtake him, and his accusers could not bear that crime for him.
rows.anchor: if he had forged such a big lie on God nothing could have saved him from the clutches of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression afāḍū means to criticize or discuss something until it is made into a mountain from a molehill.
rows.anchor: Its primary meaning is to criticize something to the extent of making a mountain of a mole-hill

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet entrusts the accusation to God, who knows the opponents’ hair-splitting and will decide whether he fabricated revelation or they deny what they know to be true.
rows.anchor: God is fully aware of the hair-splitting they are indulging in and so he has consigned this matter to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents may call the Prophet a fabricator despite knowing his honesty, simply because his message conflicts with their desires.
rows.anchor: in spite of mind him to be righteous and honest, merely because his message is against their whims and desires

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God suffices as witness; when opponents persist in obduracy and fraud against conscience, a reasonable preacher ends debate by referring the matter to Him, which may affect listeners and elevate the preacher’s standing.
rows.anchor: when it becomes evident that the contesting group is bent upon obduracy, animosity and fraud and is intentionally saying something which is against its conscience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet awaits God’s verdict with hope: any delay reflects mercy and gives deniers time to repent and mend their ways.
rows.anchor: his Lord is Gracious and Ever Merciful; He is not hasty in punishing people and in fact gives them full respite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is not the first messenger: God’s established practice is to send human messengers to human beings, so his humanity is no objection.
rows.anchor: it has remained the practice of God that to human beings, human beings are sent as messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not producing a demanded punishment does not disprove messengerhood; the Prophet claims to be a messenger, not God or a knower of the unseen.
rows.anchor: this also does not negate his claim to messengerhood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He follows revelation and serves as an open warner, claims no further responsibility, and invites debate about his actual claim rather than irrelevant demands.
rows.anchor: he is only following the revelations sent down to him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional challenge suppresses its answer to signal consequences too terrible to express if the Qur’an is from God and its rejecters persist.
rows.anchor: This suppression is pointing towards the fact that this answer encompasses such horrible consequences as are unable to be expressed in words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge asks what deniers will do if the Qur’an truly comes from God, when an Israelite witness attested to a similar revelation and believed while they acted arrogantly.
rows.anchor: a witness from the Israelites has borne testimony to such a thing, and himself professed faith in it while they are evading it out of sheer arrogance

rows.speaker: general opinion
rows.claim: The common identification makes the Israelite witness ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām.
rows.anchor: refers to ‘Abdull āh ibn Sal ām (rta)

rows.speaker: a group of scholars
rows.claim: Some scholars object that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām converted in Madīnah long after this Makkan sūrah was revealed, with no indication the verse is Madinan.
rows.anchor: a group of scholars has objected to this opinion on the grounds that he embraced Islam in Madīnah

rows.speaker: a second group of scholars
rows.claim: A second group identifies the witness as Moses.
rows.anchor: The second group thinks that this is a reference to Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects identifying the unnamed witness as Moses because succeeding verses name Moses and the Torah separately as witnesses for the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, he is mentioned by name together with the Torah separately with reference to bearing witness in favour of the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr is included among those who interpret the witness generically as the common Israelites who believed in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: This group includes Ibn Kathī r

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects a generic reading as linguistically untenable: the undefined noun magnifies the witness rather than expressing contempt or generality.
rows.anchor: To regard it to be a generic noun will be absolutely against linguistic principles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies Jesus as the Israelite witness, arguing that Jesus prepared the way for the final messenger Muhammad, the only fitting referent for the promised comer.
rows.anchor: this “comer” can only refer to him and no one else whatsoever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Gospels’ central subject is glad tidings of Muhammad; Farāhī wrote a treatise arguing that Jesus’ kingdom-of-heaven parables describe Muhammad and the Qur’anic call.
rows.anchor: The “kingdom of heaven” mentioned very frequently by Jesus (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus predicted Muhammad by name, as the Qur’an records in al-Ṣaff 6; Islahi says Gospel traits still identify him even where translations obscure them.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) has made predictions about him by actually naming him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Christians reject the Gospel of Barnabas as inauthentic, Islahi says other Gospels preserve identifying traits that honest readers recognize as Muhammad’s.
rows.anchor: other Gospels too contain a reference of the Prophet (sws). In them, though he is not mentioned by his name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi defers his fuller discussion of Jesus’ testimony to Sūrah al-Ṣaff.
rows.anchor: inshā’Allāh deal in detail with this issue in Sūrah al-Ṣaff

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus clearly described the Qur’an, its message and nature, and the stages by which its call would become dominant; Islahi also points ahead to al-Fatḥ 19.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) has mentioned very clearly the Qur’ ān, the message of the Qur’ān and the nature of this message

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus’ parable of the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone portrays God transferring the kingdom from its current holders to a people who bear its fruit.
rows.anchor: the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised enduring advocate and the powerless prince of this world are cited among Gospel testimony about the coming messenger and the triumph of his mission.
rows.anchor: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate to help you and be with you forever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mustard-seed parable depicts the gradual growth and expansion of the Islamic call until it becomes like a great tree sheltering birds.
rows.anchor: There are numerous parables which depict the gradual expansion and growth of the Islamic dawah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a fourth reason for identifying Jesus as witness, Islahi says true Nazarenes following Simon embraced the Qur’an zealously after its revelation and received Qur’anic praise.
rows.anchor: those among people who were true Nazarenes and as such were followers of Simon, the true successor of Jesus (sws) professed faith in the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mā’idah says that when Nazarenes hear the Messenger’s revelation, their eyes fill with tears because they recognize the truth and profess faith.
rows.anchor: you see their eyes fill with tears because they recognize the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi distinguishes Simon’s followers, who called themselves Nazarenes, from Paul’s followers, who rejected that label as degrading and called themselves Christians.
rows.anchor: The followers of Paul would also not call themselves as Nazarenes. They would think that this was a degrading word for them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Nazarenes’ plea to be counted among the witnesses marks them as bearers of Jesus’ testimony; their humility, unlike Paul’s followers’ conceit, enabled them to embrace Islam.
rows.anchor: Lord, we profess faith. So count us among the witnesses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects these humble followers with Jesus’ blessing for the poor in spirit and al-Mā’idah’s description of them as free from arrogance.
rows.anchor: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus’ testimony is exceptional: his mission prepared for Muhammad and the kingdom of heaven through him, conclusively informing idolaters and the People of the Book of Muhammad’s prophethood.
rows.anchor: the very objective of his prophethood was to pave the way for Muḥammad (sws) and to give glad tidings to mankind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an answers Jews and Christians backing the idolaters by pointing to an Israelite witness who testified plainly and believed; arrogant rejecters should consider their fate.
rows.anchor: a great witness from among the Israelites has already borne witness to this truth in blatant words and has professed faith in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice withholds guidance from those who wrong themselves and fail to honor the light they have received.
rows.anchor: God never guides those who wrong their souls and do not duly honour the light He blesses them with

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reason, inner and outer signs, and prophetic testimony have unveiled truth; those who misuse these sources to stray are left wandering by God.
rows.anchor: Through a person’s sense and reason and the testimony of the world within and that outside him as well through the testimony of His prophets and messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affluent rejecters treat poor people’s early acceptance as evidence against Islam, assuming that a true worldly blessing would have gone first to them.
rows.anchor: one argument they bring in their favour is that the poor were the first to accept Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After rejecting the Qur’an’s guidance, deniers call it an ancient falsehood, claiming warnings about Judgment have circulated without ever coming true.
rows.anchor: they will further say that this is not a new lie; it is one that is being transmitted from ancient times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context identifies the speakers as wealthy disbelievers and the believers as poor and destitute; their ‘old falsehood’ claim means Judgment has never appeared and will not come.
rows.anchor: the affluent among the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse presents the Torah as testimony for the Qur’an; in chronological order its evidence should have appeared earlier.
rows.anchor: This verse expresses the testimony of the Torah in favour of the Qur’ ān
